name: Electrical construction labor
description_md: Data centers are, by cost, mostly electrical construction projects — IBEW puts electrical work at 45-70% of total DC construction cost — and the US does not have the electricians to build what has been announced. The big electrical/mechanical contractors carry record books: Quanta Services $48.5B backlog (grid + DC electrical via Cupertino Electric), Comfort Systems $14.1B (+73% y/y, technology now 58% of revenue), EMCOR $17.1B RPOs (+44%). Behind them is a structural shortage: ABC estimates construction needs ~349,000 net new workers in 2026 alone, industry analyses project a shortfall approaching 500,000 workers for data-center-class construction by 2027, contractors are turning down projects outright, and hyperscalers are funding apprenticeships directly (Google's $50M IBEW program to lift enrollment from 19,500 to 30,000/year; Meta/Google/BlackRock >$265M in training). Craft labor cannot be printed: a journeyman electrician takes 4-5 years to train. Status basis: judged binding — contractors' record backlogs plus documented project refusals and 6-12-month schedule stretches show demand exceeding crew supply, and the training pipeline caps how fast supply responds.

controlled_by.share_note: Largest US specialty electrical/grid contractor; record $48.5B backlog (disclosed)
Record $14.1B backlog, +73% y/y; technology (DC) = 58% of revenue (disclosed)

dependents.dependency_md: Multi-GW self-build program competes for the same national pool of electricians and commissioning agents; labor availability now enters site selection alongside power.
Hyperion (Louisiana) and Prometheus-class builds employ thousands of electrical workers at peak; Meta co-funds training programs to expand the pipeline it draws from.
Wholesale delivery schedules depend on contracted crew availability; developers report labor as the second constraint after power in established markets.
Abilene-class campuses require thousands of tradespeople in thin rural labor markets — premium travel pay and camp logistics set the pace of buildout.

substitutes_md: Limited and slow: prefabrication/modular skids (shifting site hours to factories — Comfort Systems' modular units, Vertiv/Schneider integrated modules), overtime and traveling crews (at 1.5-2x cost), poaching from other sectors (which moves the shortage, currently hollowing out commercial/residential electrical), robots/automation (marginal for now), and training pipelines that pay off in 4-5 years. Offshoring is impossible; H-1B-style visas do not cover trades. The effective substitute is schedule slip and paying more — data-center electricians reportedly clearing $200-300k with overtime.
downcycle_md: Contractor backlogs are the canary for an AI construction downturn: unlike take-or-pay compute contracts, construction backlog is cancellable with limited penalty (typically cost-incurred plus margin on work performed), so a demand fall converts record books into air within 2-3 quarters — as happened to commercial contractors in 2008-09. Quanta is best protected (majority utility/grid work that proceeds regardless of AI), Comfort Systems most exposed (58% technology revenue). Labor itself does not glut quickly — shortage-era wage gains are sticky, and journeymen get reabsorbed by grid/reshoring/electrification demand — so a bust would hurt contractor margins and equipment suppliers more than the trades. Watch book-to-bill and the mix of signed contracts vs LOIs in reported backlog.

observations.notes: +73% y/y; technology = 58% of revenue; Q2 revenue +50%.

Up to ~499k-worker shortfall projected by 2027 for DC-class construction; ABC separately estimates 349k net new construction workers needed in 2026. Estimates vary by methodology; treat as order-of-magnitude.

sources.notes: Electrician shortage as 'life or death' threat to the AI DC boom; Google $50M IBEW program.
